title: Choose compute from the work that must run
description: Select a workload and compare candidate compute boundaries. The verdicts encode current Databricks selection guidance; they do not estimate account pricing or guaranteed performance.

workloads.label: Interactive notebook
workloads.detail: A person iterates on Python or SQL and expects responsive startup and execution.

choices.label: Serverless notebook compute
choices.detail: The documented default for most interactive notebook work.
choices.rationale: Serverless notebook compute removes cluster configuration, starts quickly, and scales automatically. Validate library, language, data-source, networking, and regional support before adopting it as the workspace default.
proof: Run representative notebooks with required libraries and data sources, including the largest shuffle and longest action.
Measure startup, interactive latency, concurrency behavior, and account billing output under normal team usage.
Verify access mode, Unity Catalog permissions, egress, and serverless feature limitations against the production contract.

choices.label: Classic all-purpose compute
choices.detail: Use when interactive work requires an unsupported serverless feature such as R or RDD APIs.
choices.rationale: Classic all-purpose compute exposes more runtime and cluster configuration, but the team owns startup, idle capacity, policy, and right-sizing. Record the feature gap that requires it instead of making it the default from habit.
proof: Name the required language, API, library, runtime, network, or configuration that serverless cannot currently provide.
Apply compute policies, an appropriate access mode, auto-termination, and bounded permissions before shared use.
Compare end-to-end productivity and idle cost with the supported serverless path.

choices.label: Classic jobs compute
choices.detail: Terminates with a job run and is not an interactive notebook default.
choices.rationale: Jobs compute is designed for automated tasks rather than an attached, person-driven notebook session. Put scheduled code in a job or choose an interactive compute type for exploration.
proof: Decide whether the work is genuinely interactive or should become a versioned, repeatable job.
If it is a job, define parameters, retries, ownership, notifications, and completion criteria.
If it is interactive, test a supported notebook compute option instead of keeping run-scoped compute alive.

workloads.label: Scheduled Python or Spark job
workloads.detail: Versioned code runs unattended and should release resources when the run completes.

choices.label: Serverless compute for jobs
choices.detail: Managed provisioning, scaling, and termination for supported job tasks.
choices.rationale: Databricks recommends serverless compute for most automated workloads. Choose the available performance mode from measured startup, runtime, and cost requirements rather than editing low-level cluster settings first.
proof: Verify every task type, library, data source, and runtime behavior is supported in serverless jobs.
Measure queue, startup, task duration, retries, and billing records over representative successful and failed runs.
Test concurrency, shuffle, skew, checkpoint recovery, and downstream side effects before production scheduling.

choices.label: Classic jobs compute
choices.detail: Use when the job requires settings or features unavailable in serverless.
choices.rationale: Classic jobs compute is the production fallback for non-SQL jobs that need custom cluster settings or unsupported serverless capabilities. It still terminates with the run, unlike an all-purpose cluster.
proof: Document the unsupported serverless capability and retest it when platform support changes.
Use a current runtime, compute policy, autoscaling bounds, and instance types justified by Spark UI evidence.
Compare job completion, failure recovery, and total billed usage with the supported serverless alternative.

choices.label: Classic all-purpose compute
choices.detail: Databricks generally advises against it for automated jobs.
choices.rationale: All-purpose compute is not optimized around the lifecycle of an automated run and can remain active after work finishes. Prefer serverless jobs or classic jobs compute so ownership and termination match the task.
proof: Move the production task to run-scoped compute and compare completion plus billed idle time.
Separate interactive troubleshooting from the scheduled production execution path.
Confirm the job can recreate every dependency from versioned configuration without a long-lived cluster.

workloads.label: BI dashboard or SQL analytics
workloads.detail: Concurrent SQL users need predictable startup, query performance, and workload isolation.

choices.label: Serverless SQL warehouse
choices.detail: Managed SQL compute for BI, ETL, and exploratory analysis.
choices.rationale: Serverless SQL warehouses are the documented default for most SQL workloads because they start and scale without customer cluster management. Size and scaling limits still need workload-specific concurrency tests.
proof: Replay representative dashboard queries with realistic concurrency, cache state, and freshness schedules.
Measure startup, queueing, p50 and tail latency, scanned bytes, scaling events, and billing output.
Verify BI connectivity, query governance, data access, network paths, and regional availability.

choices.label: Pro SQL warehouse
choices.detail: Use when serverless is unavailable or custom networking is required.
choices.rationale: A Pro SQL warehouse can satisfy SQL workloads that cannot use serverless, including documented custom-networking cases. That constraint should be explicit because startup and management behavior differ.
proof: Confirm the network or availability requirement that prevents serverless SQL use.
Load-test warehouse size and scaling limits with the real query mix and user concurrency.
Measure stopped-to-ready latency for schedules, alerts, and bursty dashboard traffic.

choices.label: Classic all-purpose compute
choices.detail: Does not provide the SQL-warehouse operating boundary expected by BI clients.
choices.rationale: A SQL warehouse is the workload-specific compute surface for Databricks SQL. Running shared production BI on an interactive Spark cluster mixes ownership, scaling, and lifecycle concerns.
proof: Connect the BI workload to a SQL warehouse and compare concurrency, queueing, and operational controls.
Separate analyst exploration from production dashboard refresh and alert schedules.
Verify query history, permissions, scaling bounds, and stop behavior on the chosen warehouse.

workloads.label: Declarative ingestion or ETL pipeline
workloads.detail: A managed pipeline materializes streaming tables or views with quality expectations.

choices.label: Serverless pipeline compute
choices.detail: Managed infrastructure for supported Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines.
choices.rationale: Serverless is the documented default for most pipelines and removes classic cluster configuration. The pipeline still needs explicit data contracts, expectations, checkpoint behavior, and operational ownership.
proof: Verify connectors, libraries, sources, sinks, and pipeline features against current serverless support.
Test full refresh, incremental restart, late data, schema drift, expectation failures, and backfill behavior.
Measure source backlog, update duration, data quality, freshness, and billing output.

choices.label: Classic pipeline compute
choices.detail: Use for unsupported serverless features or legacy Hive metastore requirements.
choices.rationale: Classic pipeline compute is appropriate when a required capability is unavailable in serverless or the pipeline still depends on the legacy Hive metastore. Keep the exception visible and plan its review.
proof: Name the exact unsupported feature or legacy metastore dependency and assign a migration owner.
Constrain runtime, worker bounds, access mode, policies, libraries, and network configuration as code.
Retest serverless compatibility during runtime and platform upgrades.

choices.label: Manually run notebook cluster
choices.detail: Lacks the repeatable pipeline lifecycle and unattended recovery contract.
choices.rationale: A production pipeline should have versioned configuration, an execution identity, retries, notifications, and observable update state. A notebook attached to a shared cluster is an authoring surface, not that operating contract.
proof: Move pipeline code and configuration into version control and deploy it repeatably across environments.
Define schedule or event triggers, retries, notifications, ownership, and completion criteria.
Prove recovery from partial writes, checkpoint loss, schema change, and source replay without manual notebook state.
